query: Which method can be used for high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: In situ high‐temperature X‐ray diffraction (HTXRD) is an effective method to study both the oxidation behavior and phase stability of high-entropy alloys at elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., CrMnFeCoNi HEA) with a well‐defined face‐centered cubic (FCC) structure in the as‐cast or homogenized condition.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the HEA to high-temperature oxidation conditions (in air or controlled atmospheres) while continuously collecting XRD data.
generation.conditions: Operating temperatures within the range relevant to high-temperature applications (approximately 750–1320 °C as indicated by thermodynamic stability ranges) under in situ conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Phase formation and transformations (e.g., oxidation product formation and possible solid-solution decomposition evidenced by shifts or emergence of diffraction peaks).
generation.mechanism: In situ HTXRD enables real-time monitoring of lattice reflections, thereby revealing changes in phase composition and the kinetics of oxide layer formation. This allows correlation between oxidation kinetics and phase stability with the underlying thermodynamic predictions (often modeled by CALPHAD).
generation.predicted_outcome: The obtained XRD patterns will show time- and temperature-dependent changes that correlate with the formation of non-protective or protective oxide phases and eventual phase decomposition/restructuring of the HEA, confirming the stability window predicted by computational methods.
generation.baseline: Ex situ characterization methods, in which samples are quenched and analyzed after oxidation, may miss transient phase changes and oxidation kinetics.
generation.boundary: The method’s effectiveness might be limited for very minor phases or for phases with low diffraction intensity; also, extreme conditions beyond the calibrated temperature range could reduce accuracy.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative determination of the amount of each phase and the kinetics of phase transitions may be affected by resolution limits and overlapping peaks, leading to uncertainty in distinguishing closely related phases.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of CrMnFeCoNi HEA samples and subject them to a well-controlled high-temperature oxidation experiment while continuously monitoring their phase evolution using in situ XRD. In parallel, perform ex situ XRD after identical thermal exposures. Compare the real-time phase evolution and oxidation kinetics observed in situ with both the ex situ results and the predictions from CALPHAD simulations.
measurements: Time-resolved XRD diffraction patterns during high-temperature exposure
Phase identification and quantification (e.g., FCC phase, oxide phases) from diffraction peaks
Post-exposure microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM/EDS) to verify oxide scale formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the in situ XRD does not detect the expected time-dependent phase transitions or oxidation products (as predicted by CALPHAD and confirmed by ex situ measurements), or if the method fails to capture transient changes that are critical to understanding oxidation behavior, then the hypothesis that in situ HTXRD is effective for studying high-temperature oxidation and phase stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. 4.1. Phase Stability at High Temperature

HEAs produced on casting when exposed to long-term annealing cause decomposition into the traditional multi-phase microstructure. The alloys decomposition on annealing at a higher temperature creates doubt about its applicability for high-temperature application (over 800 °C). Thermodynamic calculations were performed to understand whether the solid solution established when cast is a thermodynamically stable phase at potential use temperatures. Phase equilibria of CrMnFeCoNi alloy are visualized in Figure 9 as a one-dimensional step diagram of phase fractions and a function of temperature. From Figure 9 the critical features of phase equilibria are readily discernible, such as the thickness of the HEA’s single-phase FCC region (solvus to the solidus) at high temperature from solidus at 1320 °C down to about 750 °C. Also, it shows the lower temperature decomposition products stated in some works. At a lower temperature, phase equilibria show the formation of the sigma phase and BCC phase.
